rv.q: And for 70 minutes it feels like we know Sarah Kane too, like she exists in this room, in all her darkness and brilliance.
This quietly brilliant production by James Macdonald, still definitive in my view, is less literal and embraces the musicality of the piece.
This is a must-see revival of the searing last play by Sarah Kane...
The attention to such fine details in James Macdonald’s rich production is exquisite.
This is a stark, brave drama from a truly remarkable playwright; 25 years on, it still devastates.

I came out of the Court feeling subdued, sad and unenlightened, but writing this hours later in a bright dawn, I find the play's combative humanity and its striking final image of escape have stayed with me.
But this production feels like the reconstruction of a seminal performance rather than a seminal performance for today.
This production is an exercise in the actor’s craft, an exquisitely wrought gilt frame surrounding an empty canvas.
The artists and creatives behind the production truly understand the work and its nature of nonlinear form.
If this particular production now seems muted, it is still a theatrical highlight of 2025, offering audiences a portal onto a monumental event in recent theatre history.
This current reboot, which remains powerful enough to leave me shaken, also seals the play in the aspic of commemoration.

Psychology students and phantom attendees at funerals will love it, otherwise, save the ticket price and instead go and educate yourself about Sarah and her struggles, which may prove a far more worthwhile exercise.

cn.t: Kane's searing final play retains its devastating power 25 years on, with critics praising its raw emotional impact and the original cast's return, though some question the lack of fresh interpretation in this nostalgic recreation.
